summary: Outcome series found and saved in D:/Workspace/inter-trade-present/data/steel_route/. (1) Route: Germany crude steel by oxygen/electric route 1999-2025 (kt, shares) from worldsteel yearbooks 2009/2018/2019-20, World Steel in Figures 2021 and WV Stahl revision tables 2021-2025; electric-arc share is flat: 29.2% (1999), 30.5% (2025, WV Stahl revision; 30.6% worldsteel), range 27.7% (2023) to 34.7% (2009); 2020 kt missing (only 35.7 Mt and 32.3% published). (2) ETS: DEHSt/UBA verified emissions of 'Eisen und Stahl' for every year 2005-2025, in three installation scopes that must not be compared across breaks (A 2005-07, B 2008-12, C 2013-25); scope C: 35.65 Mt (2013) -> 37.9 (2018) -> 35.6 (2019) -> 30.0 (2025). (3) Derived CO2 per tonne of crude steel (scope C): 0.84 (2013) -> 0.88 (2025), range 0.84-0.92, no fall; independent WV Stahl specific CO2 (incl. purchased power): 1.59 (1990), 1.37 (2019), 1.39 (2025). Absolute ETS emissions fell 15.7% 2019-2025 only because crude steel fell 13.5%. Route level (DEHSt, direct): blast-furnace route about 1.05-1.08 t CO2e per t oxygen steel vs electric-arc about 0.09. Free allocation context 2019-2024 and EU27 comparison (electric share 45.8%) included. Live DEHSt server and the EEA ETS datastore were down on 2026-10-22, so DEHSt reports came from Internet Archive copies of the official PDFs and the EEA installation-level file was not used. All numbers were asserted against the cited page text.

discrepancies_vs_workbook: Dataset A 2024: workbook 37.2 Mt (WV Stahl brochures / Destatis); WV Stahl crude-steel table, revision July 2025, gives 37,310 kt (37.3 Mt): +0.11 Mt (+0.3%). Both vintages are official; the brochure value is the earlier one.

Dataset A 2025: workbook 34.1 Mt (worldsteel; WV Stahl preliminary 34,090 kt; also printed in WV Stahl brochure of 2026-10-08); WV Stahl revision of August 2026 gives 34,267 kt (34.3 Mt): +0.18 Mt (+0.5%). Route split in the workbook, 69.4% oxygen / 30.6% electric, is confirmed on the Germany row of worldsteel World Steel in Figures 2026 p.10 (and 69.36/30.64 in the WV Stahl preliminary release); the revision table gives 69.5 / 30.5.

Dataset A 2017-2023 (43.3, 42.4, 39.6, 35.7, 40.2, 36.9, 35.4 Mt) agree with the worldsteel yearbook and WV Stahl revision tables after rounding (43,297; 42,435; 39,627; 35.7; 40,241; 36,861; 35,395 kt): no discrepancy.

Source citation: workbook S12 cites the WV Stahl brochure 2025 (printed p.9, chart 2011-2024). A newer edition (Daten und Fakten 2026, published 2026-10-08, printed p.9, chart 2012-2025 including 34.1 Mt in 2025) is available and should replace it for 2025.

Coincidence to keep apart: the workbook figure 69.4% is Germany's oxygen share (correct); the world-average BOF share in the same worldsteel publication is also 69.4% (WSIF 2026 PDF p.4, and 'total of above countries' on p.10).

Outline S12 'covered ETS emissions about 50% below 2005 in 2024 [U29]' is an EU aggregate (power-led). German iron and steel installations are not comparable that way: DEHSt consistent-scope text says about +2% in 2017 and -9% in 2019 vs 2005; scope-C emissions 2025 (30.0 Mt) are 16% below 2019 only because crude steel is 13.5% lower.
Outline S10 Q row and S8 tile stop at crude steel 2024 (37.2 Mt); data now exist for 2025 (34.1 Mt preliminary, 34.3 Mt revised).

caveats: Scope breaks in the DEHSt sector row: first period 2005-2006 (2007 transitional), second period 2008-2012, third period 2013-2025 (about 80 extra mostly processing plants). Levels are comparable only inside a segment; the derived ratio jump 0.73 (2012) to 0.84 (2013) is the scope change. DEHSt publishes a scope-adjusted series only as an unlabelled chart, with the text statements +2% (2005-2017) and -9% (2005-2019).

The ETS iron-and-steel row excludes process-gas emissions released at power plants (16.8-21.8 Mt in the years read: 2013, 2014, 2019, 2020), contains coke ovens, sintering and rolling plants, covers direct emissions only (no purchased electricity). The WV Stahl series has a different boundary (incl. purchased power, excl. coke ovens); only trends should be compared.

Utilisation effect: blast-furnace emissions are largely fixed, so the per-tonne ratio rises when output falls (2023: 0.92). Route share is only a proxy (scrap supply, product mix, plant closures; 2009 peak is a recession artefact) and is not hydrogen-based direct reduction, which has not started in Germany.

Precision and vintages: 2023 and 2025 ETS values only to 0.1 Mt; 2007 derived from the 2008 report comparison set; 2020 crude steel only to 0.1 Mt and 2020 route kt missing; DEHSt restates 0.1-0.4 Mt between reports; crude steel 2024 and 2025 have two official vintages; WSIF 2018 edition gave a 2017 estimate (28.8% electric) later replaced by 30.0%.

Access: dehst.de returned a maintenance page and the EEA ETS datastore failed (HTTP 400/503) on 2026-10-22. DEHSt VET reports 2006, 2008-2024 were taken from Internet Archive copies of the official PDFs (timestamps in sources_manifest.csv); no 2007 or 2025 VET report was reachable, so 2025 rests on the UBA table of 2026-09-24 (DEHSt data, Stand 05/2026). The EEA installation-level file would allow a scope-consistent series and should be retried.

Descriptive only: nothing here identifies an effect of the ETS or CBAM; CBAM payments start in 2027; trade (imports, exports, consumption) is not netted out. Free-allocation ratios are inflated by allowances passed on for forwarded process gases (nominal 128-144%, adjusted 83.5-108%); no 2025 allocation figure obtained.

Derived values (ETS emissions per tonne, route emissions per tonne, shares from kt) are my arithmetic on published figures and are labelled DERIVED in the files; the 2020 route output used for route emissions per tonne is derived from 35.7 Mt times the published 67.7/32.3 split.
